Q: Selecting from a temporary #table whose column is sp_renamed has stopped working for SQL Server version 2019 and later A:

If you insert the statement SELECT * FROM TempDB.sys.columns WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('tempdb..#headerX') ORDER BY column_id immediately after the EXEC sp_rename ..., you will see that the column is in fact renamed. The problem seems to be that SQL Server initially recognizes the need to defer compilation of the query following the sp_rename, but then reuses that compiled code for later executions, assuming that the parameter value changes are not significant.

Yes, this does appear to be an breaking change from 2017 to 2019 that is not listed in the breaking change documentation, but one where the WITH RECOMPILE option seems to the obvious fix.

I believe you have the following options:

  1. Add WITH RECOMPILE to the stored procedure definition.
  2. Add WITH RECOMPILE to the EXEC ... that executes the stored procedure.
  3. Add OPTION(RECOMPILE) to the specific query that is misbehaving. (Credit to the OP for identifying and implementing this option - likely the best choice.)
  4. Rewrite your code as you did for the #headerY case.

See this db<>fiddle. The different options can be tested by uncommenting the appropriate lines labeled "option #1" - "option #4" and/or changing the selected SQL Server version to compare results.

Q: Return value in a Bash function A:

I know eval is frowned upon, however I use this, an example function also ensuring there is a returned value should prevent malicious inputs:

example usage:

input-required "Enter your email to personalise" emailtest

with input being "some@email.com"

this value is available in the variable $emailtest:

echo $emailtest

testmail.com

#ensure input is not blank
#the second argument is the variable to put the input into, also the value is available as $INPUT
function input-required() {
  prompt="$1"
  returnvar="$2"
  if [[ -z "$prompt" ]]; then
    prompt='Enter a value'
  fi
  while true; do
    # if counter is equal to 2 exit
    read -p "$prompt : " INPUT
    if [[ -z "$INPUT" ]]; then
      echo "Error! Input cannot be empty"
      continue
    fi
    break
  done
  evalcmd="$returnvar=$INPUT"
  eval "$evalcmd"
}

Q: Fix narrowing warning A:

Notice that the .length() method returns an unsigned datatype. To fix this you can do:

int length1[2] = { (int)schemaName.length() + 2, (int)tableName.length() + 2 };

This casts the unsigned integer into a signed integer, eliminating the warning. You just have to make sure that there will not be integer overflow.

Q: Is it possible to unload a QML object loaded with QQmlApplicationEngine::load()? A:

There is not direct unload, but you can have the same effect by destorying the root objects.

for (QObject* obj : engine.rootObjects())
    delete obj;

Of you can use a Loader as the root element and set its source to "" so its child will be "unloaded"

Q: Invoke-Sqlcmd times out after ~30s on some machines but not others (without -QueryTimeout). What determines the default and what’s best practice? A:

AlwaysLearning provided the crucial pointer in a comment on the question:

Your symptom suggests that different machines of yours use different editions of the Invoke-SqlCmd cmdlet:

There are two - technically distinct - Invoke-SqlCmd cmdlets:[1]

  • (a) The obsolete Invoke-SqlCmd command from the obsolete SQLPS module.

  • (b) The current Invoke-SqlCmd command from the successor module, SqlServer

    • The SqlServer module can be installed from the PowerShell Gallery with, e.g.: Install-Module -Scope CurrentUser SqlServer

You can tell which version is loaded (implicitly) on a given machine by running the following command in a pristine session:

(Get-Command Invoke-SqlCmd).Module

  • Implementation (a) de facto appears to default to 30 seconds.

    • The official help topic is, as of this writing, malformed and is missing a description of the -QueryTimeout parameter (a description of the command as a whole is presented instead).

    • It's hard to find definitive claims to that effect, but here's a pointer from Troubleshoot query time-out errors:

      • If the query doesn't return any data within the configured time-out value (typically 30 seconds)

  • By contrast, implementation (b) defaults to not timing out, based on the official help topic stating for the -QueryTimeout parameter:

    • If a timeout value is not specified, the queries do not time out.

[1] See SQL Server PowerShell for background information.
